title: Could Homework Widen the Gap Between Families?
paragraphs: Homework has long enjoyed the status of an unexamined good, yet a new paper from the University of Manchester invites us to ask whom it really serves. Published in the British Journal of Sociology of Education, the study scrutinises the assumption that parents have time to spare for their children's schoolwork, and finds it wanting.

The evidence is deliberately narrow: an in-depth case study of one mother, Emma, who works until 8pm, and her child's teacher, Mrs Higgins, written by an author who was herself a parent at the school. Drawing on Bourdieu, the team frames parental time as a form of cultural capital, one that is unevenly spread. Better-resourced families can offset the pressure with private tutoring; others are left to cope with homework that, in the authors' account, can feel stressful or shaming. Dr Emilia Howker puts it plainly: "Some parents simply have more time and resources available to them."

What makes the argument sharper is its refusal of an easy remedy. Abolishing homework might merely displace the burden, since other forms of parental engagement would rush in to fill the gap; the real task, as Professor Laura Black suggests, is to rethink what we expect of parents at all. Readers should keep the limits in view, however: one case cannot be extrapolated at will, and the press release is silent on funding.

questions.q: What assumption does the paper challenge?
questions.a: That parents have time to spare for their children's schoolwork.

questions.q: Why might abolishing homework merely displace the burden?
questions.a: Other forms of parental engagement would fill the gap.

questions.q: What limits should readers keep in mind?
questions.a: The study rests on one case and the release does not mention funding.
